idiom_name: public method outline + private methods (expression-bodied steps)
implementation_notes: C# keeps the classic shape directly: the public method's body is an outline of private method calls, and expression-bodied members (`T M() => expression;`) make a one-line step read exactly like the sentence it replaces in the outline. What the language adds since C# 7 is the local function: a helper used by exactly one method is declared inside it, stays invisible to the rest of the type, and - unlike a lambda assigned to `Func<>` - is not converted to a delegate when it is only called, so it allocates nothing. Prefer private methods when several methods share a step or a subclass should override it; prefer expression bodies for pure single-expression steps and a `static` local function when the helper must not capture the enclosing state.
pitfalls: Wrap a step in `Func<>`/`Action` (or assign a lambda to a delegate) and the compiler allocates a closure plus a delegate per call; keep steps as methods or local functions and convert to a delegate only at the boundary that needs one.

A `private` step is not an extension point: subclasses cannot override it and same-assembly tests reach it by reflection - decide explicitly between `private` (implementation detail) and `protected virtual` (an override hook), because changing that later breaks derived types.

A step whose expression body returns `IEnumerable<T>` is a deferred query: `=> _lines.Where(..)` re-executes on every enumeration, so materialize with `ToList()` or return `IReadOnlyList<T>` when the outline names a computed result.

variants.name: Local-function steps (C# 7)
variants.idiom_name: local functions declared inside the composed method
variants.implementation_notes: Microsoft's local-function guidance makes the helper of a single caller a nested declaration: it can only be called from its containing member, cannot carry an access modifier (all local functions are private), and is only converted to a delegate when it is actually used as one, so the call stays a plain static call. Use this variant when the steps exist only for one outline (parsing a request shape, a recursive walk), when the helper needs the outline's locals without widening them into parameters, or when you want the steps to disappear with the method. Promote a step to a private method as soon as a second caller appears or a subclass must replace it - local functions cannot be overridden and are invisible to the type.
pitfalls: A local function that is converted to a delegate (stored in a `Func<>`, subscribed to an event) captures the enclosing method's state and allocates; keep it a direct call while it stays local.

Local functions are visible only inside the containing member, so the day a second method needs the step it must be promoted to a private method and any captured local has to become a parameter; design the helper as if that promotion will happen.
